entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sebastian z Felsztyna, born in Felsztyn (modern Skelivka, Ukraine) in an unknown year and dying in 1544, emerged as the preeminent Polish composer and music theorist of the early 16th century, a pivotal figure in solidifying the foundations of Renaissance music in Eastern Europe. His contributions, particularly in the realm of sacred polyphony and didactic musical texts, positioned him as a central intellectual force within the Jagiellonian court and the broader scholarly environment of Kraków. His work reflects the stylistic currents of the Franco-Flemish school, adapting them to a distinct Polish context and contributing to the rich cultural tapestry of the Polish Golden Age under the Jagiellonian dynasty.

A graduate of the prestigious Jagiellonian University around 1507, Sebastian z Felsztyna's active career primarily unfolded in Kraków, where he likely served as a choirmaster or organist. His most significant surviving works include several motets, such as 'Alleluia, Felix es sacra virgo Maria' and 'Alleluia, Ave Maria', which exemplify sophisticated contrapuntal techniques characteristic of the high Renaissance. Beyond composition, his lasting impact stems from his theoretical treatises, notably 'Opusculum musices noviter congestum' (1517) and 'Directiones musicae ad cathedralis ecclesiae metropolitanae Gnesnensis usum' (1539). These texts were among the earliest printed works on music theory in Poland, providing practical instruction on plainsong, mensural notation, and counterpoint, thereby standardizing musical education and practice in the region.
